headline: WEEKEND EDITION. Chair Warsh's first Jackson Hole keynote triggered the year's largest hawkish repricing: a September HIKE is now the base case at 59% on our own CME payload, from 37.6% Thursday, and 2s10s bear-flattened 7.1bp. Semis took the hit at -3.47% while the VIX FELL to 14.43. Post-close Friday, Trump announced a 65-billion-barrel Venezuela oil agreement with no mechanics released
client_frame_short:
The question you will get Monday: "Did the Fed just change direction?" On Friday morning the new Chair, Kevin Warsh, gave his first Jackson Hole speech and said the quiet part out loud - inflation is the bigger worry, and the central bank owns it. The bond market repriced hard: the odds of a rate HIKE in September jumped to 59% from 38% in an afternoon. **The market now expects the Fed's next move to be up, not down.**

Nothing here needs a decision from you. Two things are worth knowing. This was a bond event, not a stock event - two-year yields rose 11 basis points while the S&P slipped a quarter of a percent and still finished the week higher. And the pain was concentrated: semiconductors fell 3.5% Friday, and Nvidia gave back half of Thursday's jump to finish the week up just 1.3%.
client_frame:
Friday was the most consequential day of Chair Warsh's tenure so far, and the reason is worth stating precisely because the headline numbers understate it. In his first Jackson Hole keynote he said that on the price-stability side of the mandate the numbers are more concerning, that 2% is a firm, fixed target, and - the line that did the damage - that we must be confident underlying inflation is moving to our objective clearly and at sufficient speed, otherwise we have work to do. He put the blame squarely on the institution he now runs, saying the responsibility for 65 months of sustained elevated inflation sits squarely with the central bank. He noted 54% of the goods and services in the consumption basket are rising faster than 3%, against 32% before the pandemic. He said labour markets are consistent with full employment and financial conditions are not broadly restrictive, which removes both of the usual arguments against tightening. And he explicitly refused to give a reaction function, saying he stands committed to a discipline and not to a decision. Every one of those quotes is from the Fed's own transcript.

The rate market took him at his word. On our own re-derived CME payload a 25bp HIKE at the September 16 meeting is now the base case at 59.00%, up from 37.64% on Thursday, with October at 71.71%, December at 89.46% and January at 92.12%. The single most telling change is December's odds of two or more hikes, which went from 29.84% to 51.81% - the market moved from a coin-flip on one more hike to a coin-flip on two. Cut probability is exactly zero at every meeting through January 2027. Two-year yields rose 11.4bp to 4.352% while the 30-year added only 1.1bp, so the curve bear-flattened and 2s10s went to 36.5bp from 43.6bp. Gold fell 3.03%, its worst session since February, and broke its 200-day average. Bitcoin gave back about 2%. I will name a spread rather than pick a number: the wires put September's odds anywhere from 55.5% to about 60%, and 59.00% is what our own payload says.

Now the part that is genuinely odd and is the most useful observation in this note. Equities did not care in aggregate and the volatility market cared even less. The S&P fell 0.25% and the Dow was unchanged. The VIX FELL to 14.43, traded as high as 14.84 and fully round-tripped, and the Nasdaq-100 volatility index closed at 19.92 - its lowest close since January 12 on our own two-year series. Front-to-three-month VIX is still in steep contango at 0.8255. But underneath the index the damage was real and narrow: semiconductors fell 3.47%, Marvell 10.28% on soft fiscal-2028 guidance, Nvidia 4.58%. Breadth was far worse than the headline, with 1,791 advancers against 2,888 decliners and only 37% of issues higher. PayPal fell 12.71% after Stripe and Advent walked away from a roughly $50 billion approach; Gap rose 12.94% on a beat and a raised forecast. When the equity market and the rate market disagree this cleanly, the disagreement itself is the observation - and the carry crosses agree with the calm reading, since EUR/JPY and AUD/JPY were both unchanged, which is not what a stress event looks like.

For the week the scoreboard was quietly positive and thinly led: the S&P rose 0.49%, the Dow 0.53% and snapped a two-week losing streak, the Nasdaq 100 rose 0.43%, and the Russell 2000 fell 1.5%. Only four of eleven sectors finished higher. The semiconductor index fell 2.31% in the same week its largest member reported 117% data-centre growth, and Nvidia itself, one day after its third-best session in two years, finished the week up just 1.32%. Investors pulled $22.33 billion from US equity funds through Aug 26, the largest weekly outflow since March, and put $7.12 billion into bonds. Two things to watch into Monday. First, the buried release: the BLS preliminary payroll benchmark revision for March 2026 came in at MINUS 79,000, a non-event next to last year's minus 911,000 and actually below the ten-year average revision - but it was published the same minute Warsh began speaking, so no market move is cleanly attributable to it, and we are saying that rather than attributing it. Second, Friday night the President announced an agreement for the US to control 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan reserves, with no agreement or mechanics released by the White House; crude settled Friday down slightly and more than 4% lower on the week. For clients: the frame this weekend is that the Fed has stopped pretending its next move might be a cut, and the market agrees with it - which makes next Friday's jobs report, eleven days before the FOMC, the most important number on the calendar, and makes this a good moment to check that a portfolio is positioned for a higher-for-longer path rather than for the rate cuts nobody is pricing any more.

single_name_moves.note: $216.62, -10.28% on our own settled bars, the worst large-cap move of the day and the clearest evidence that Friday's equity damage was about AI capital spending rather than about the Fed. Marvell guided fiscal 2028 below expectations and gave no timing on its Google AI-chip work. It is now 31.543% below its 6/4/26 record close of 316.43 and fell 8.61% on the week. Reconciled rather than reported as a conflict: a CNBC piece carrying minus 6% was a premarket snapshot, not the close

$217.55, -4.58%, and this is the single best client line of the week when you put it next to Thursday. Thursday's +8.74% was its third-best session in two years. Friday gave back more than half of it, and the stock finished the WEEK up just 1.32% - best day in sixteen months, and a 1.3% week. Q2 revenue was $96.2bn with data centre at $89bn, up 117% year over year, so this is not a demand problem. It is a valuation and expectations problem, and it is still 7.716% below its 5/14/26 record close of 235.74

$53.66, -12.71% on volume 124% above normal, after Stripe and Advent abandoned a takeover approach valued around $50 billion. The largest single-name loss of the day had nothing to do with the Fed and everything to do with a deal disappearing, which is a useful reminder that on any given day the loudest mover is usually idiosyncratic

About $23.48, +12.94%, on an earnings beat, full-year guidance raised to $2.35-2.45 and a new Old Navy chief executive. The exception that keeps the pattern honest: a hawkish Fed day still paid a beat-and-raise handsomely, so this was not a tape that refused all good news

geo_headlines: THE FED CHAIR MADE A HIKE THE BASE CASE AND WE ARE REPORTING OUR OWN PAYLOAD, NOT THE WIRE SPREAD: on our re-derived CME cohort dated 2026-08-28, all four meetings summing to 1.0000, a 25bp HIKE on September 16 is now 59.00% against 37.64% on Thursday - a 21.4 point move in one afternoon, the largest single-day hawkish repricing of 2026. Hold is 41.00%. October cumulative hike odds 71.71% from 52.83%, December 89.46% from 75.16%, January 2027 92.12% from 80.29%. The most substantive change is December's odds of TWO OR MORE hikes: 51.81% from 29.84%. Cut probability is exactly ZERO at every meeting through January 2027. Wire prints for September range from 55.5% (Guardian) through 57.5% (CNBC) to about 60% (Yahoo, Reuters); we name the spread and ship 59.00% because it is ours and we can show the arithmetic.

WHAT WARSH ACTUALLY SAID, FROM THE FED'S OWN TRANSCRIPT RATHER THAN FROM A PARAPHRASE: the money quote is that we must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed, otherwise we have work to do. He called 2% PCE a firm, fixed target, said that on the price-stability side of our mandate the numbers are more concerning, cited 12-month PCE at 3.7% and six-month at 4.1%, and noted that 54 percent of goods and services in the PCE basket showed price increases above 3 percent against 32% pre-pandemic. He said the responsibility for 65 months of sustained, elevated inflation sits squarely with the central bank. He removed both standard objections to tightening: labour markets are consistent with full employment, and financial conditions are not broadly restrictive. He refused a reaction function or a Taylor rule - I stand here today committed to a discipline, not to a decision - and said he has set out to change the form and function of the Chairman's forward guidance so that market participants stop looking primarily to the Fed for their next trade, calling it a hall-of-mirrors problem. BMO's read: a deliberately hawkish speech that puts to rest any concerns about the Fed's willingness to raise rates.

THE DIVERGENCE IS THE OBSERVATION: SEMIS TOOK A 3.47% HIT WHILE THE VOLATILITY MARKET WENT BACK TO SLEEP. The SOX fell 3.47%, Marvell 10.28%, Nvidia 4.58% - and the VIX FELL to 14.43, -0.55%. It traded as high as 14.84 intraday and fully round-tripped, which is the best tape detail of the day. VXN closed 19.92, -1.58%, its LOWEST CLOSE SINCE 2026-01-12 verified over our own 501 daily bars, and -9.37% on the week. Front-to-three-month VIX is 14.43/17.48 = 0.8255 against 0.8263 Thursday: still steep contango, still complacency. Both yen carry crosses were unchanged, EUR/JPY -0.01% and AUD/JPY -0.01%, so FX agrees with the calm reading and not with the semis. Breadth agreed with the semis instead: 1,791 advancers against 2,888 decliners, 37% of issues higher, net minus 1,097, with a liquid-subset median of -1.27% - two independent breadth sources agreeing. One conflict disclosed: Doug Kass published the VIX at 14.39/-0.83% while Cboe, Yahoo and Investing say 14.43.

THE CURVE BEAR-FLATTENED, WHICH IS THE SHAPE THAT SAYS POLICY RATHER THAN INFLATION EXPECTATIONS: the 2-year settled 4.352%, +11.4bp, while the 30-year added only 1.1bp to 5.207%, so 2s10s went to 36.5bp from 43.6bp - 7.1bp of flattening. The whole front end moved: 1Y 4.145% +12.3bp, 6M 3.984% +7.7bp, 3M 3.824% +5.0bp. Attributed and not asserted: WSJ and Dow Jones called the 2-year's +0.118pp the largest single-day yield gain following a Jackson Hole Chair speech since Greenspan in 1996, which is their claim on their basis. We also log a data defect for the record: TradingEconomics' dedicated 10Y page read 4.69/+0.01pp in both content and description meta while TE's OWN overview table read 4.717/+0.043, TE /bonds read 4.7170, and CNBC, WSJ, Reuters and Fidelity all read 4.72-4.73. The dedicated page matches a 10:27 ET intraday snapshot and is LAGGED, so it is logged DEGRADED and we ship 4.717 - the reverse of our usual preference, recorded rather than quietly dropped.

THE BURIED NUMBER, AND THE HONEST LIMIT ON WHAT WE CAN SAY ABOUT IT: the BLS published its PRELIMINARY payroll benchmark revision for March 2026 at MINUS 79,000, or -0.1%, with total private at minus 178,000, release USDL-26-1425. That is a non-event beside last year's minus 911,000 preliminary and it is BELOW the ten-year average absolute revision of 0.2%. Implied monthly job growth falls to roughly plus 11,000 from about plus 18,000; the final benchmark arrives in February 2027. Largest downward moves were retail trade minus 154,600 and private education and health minus 96,000, with transportation and warehousing revised UP 135,100 and government up 99,000. Now the limit: it was released at 10:00 ET, the same minute the Chair began speaking, so no market move is cleanly attributable to it. It is reaction-OBSCURED, not reaction-free, and we are saying so instead of attributing anything to it. Discarded for the record: one crypto outlet reported the revision as UPWARD, which contradicts the BLS release outright.

THE UNPRICED WEEKEND HEADLINE IS AN OIL HEADLINE, AND IT CUTS AGAINST WARSH'S OWN COMMODITY WARNING: at 9:28 PM ET Friday, after the close, President Trump announced on Truth Social that the US has entered an agreement to take control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan proven reserves - the biggest oil deal in world history in his words - negotiated by Rubio and Hegseth with interim President Delcy Rodriguez, at no cost to the American taxpayer, and more than doubling American oil reserves. The White House has released NO agreement and NO mechanics; Rodriguez separately cites $209 billion flowing to Venezuelan coffers. This is live gap risk in crude into Tuesday and it sits directly against Warsh's own line that the recent rise in overall commodity prices bears watching. Pushing the other way: Treasury moved Friday to cut roughly $1.8 billion of Iranian shadow-banking flows through Banque Misr's UAE branches, covering 103 companies from January 2024 to June 2026 - reported by the NY Post, with NO matching treasury.gov release found, so it is reported and not primary-confirmed.

THE WEEK IN ONE PARAGRAPH, AND IT WAS NARROWER THAN THE INDEX LEVEL SUGGESTS: S&P +0.49%, Dow +0.53% snapping a two-week losing streak, Nasdaq 100 +0.43%, Nasdaq Composite +0.8% (Investopedia says +0.9%), Russell 2000 -1.5% and closing Friday on its low. Only FOUR of eleven sectors finished the week higher - technology +1.8%, communication services +1.6%, financials +1.1%, consumer discretionary +0.1% - while health care and energy fell 2%, industrials 1.7% and real estate 1.3%. Best performers were Salesforce +22% and CrowdStrike +14%; worst were Boston Scientific -7% and EOG -6.3%. The semiconductor index fell 2.31% in the same week its largest member reported 117% data-centre growth. Investors pulled $22.33 billion from US equity funds in the week through Aug 26, the largest weekly outflow since March, against $7.12 billion of bond inflows. August is still +3% for the S&P and the index is up about 13% year to date. Two weekly numbers are excluded on purpose: one wealth-manager page carrying +1.82%/+1.54%/+1.18% is contradicted by the AP wire and its own URL says week ending Aug 21.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY ON THE CALENDAR, VERIFIED AGAINST ISSUERS, PLUS THE ONE THING NOBODY SHOULD MIS-DIARISE: Saturday and Sunday are CONFIRMED EMPTY against BLS, the Fed, BEA and Treasury. There is NO US market holiday between Monday Aug 31 and Friday Sep 4 and no early close - Labor Day 2026 is Monday SEPT 7, confirmed on nyse.com, nasdaqtrader.com, FINRA, Nasdaq and Fidelity. Monday is a normal full session and is also month-end, so rebalancing and settlement flows will carry part of the tape. Tuesday brings ISM manufacturing (July 55.6%) and JOLTS (June 7.359mn) at 10:00, plus Dell after the close. Wednesday brings ADP (July +44,000) and the Beige Book at 2:00. Thursday brings claims, the trade balance, revised productivity and ISM services (July 54.1%). Friday Sept 4 at 8:30 brings the AUGUST EMPLOYMENT REPORT - triple-verified on the BLS empsit page, the BLS September schedule and the NY Fed calendar - with consensus around plus 60,000 and 4.1% unemployment against July's MINUS 23,000. It lands eleven days before the Sept 15-16 FOMC and into pre-holiday liquidity. Also that week: Michigan final August sentiment printed 51.7 on Friday, revised UP from 51.0 but still down 11.2% year over year on inflation fears, which sits awkwardly beside Warsh calling medium-term expectations stable.
